extracted.intended_audience: readers of Charles Lamb / general literary readers and scholars of 19th-century letters
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and production of Charles Lamb's Elia letters/essays, with incidental prescriptive remarks about handwriting, epistolary style, titling, and literary taste embedded in the letters. Useful for editorial, literary-critical, or stylistic guidance within this genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, bold handwriting in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: I like a clear letter; a bold, free hand and a fearless flourish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with 'mean, detestable' hands that look like begging letters. Avoid 'figurantes' numerals that stagger, 'erring' ruled lines that threaten to meet, and timid blots; a bold, free hand and a decisive flourish (e.g., a corkscrew) are recommended to 'fill up' and improve an epistle's appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interlineations and visible corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: She is sure to omit a most substantial word in the second draught (for she never ventures an epistle without a foul copy first), which is obliged to be interlined,—which spoils the neatest epistle, you know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a procedure that leaves interlined insertions in the fair copy; such visible corrections harm the neatness and impression of a letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dot i's and cross t's; finish letters cleanly
rubrics_metrics.description: Then she has always to go through them (a second operation) to dot her i's and cross her t's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to small finishing details in handwriting and correspondence, as they contribute materially to the letter's neatness and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin letters directly; avoid excessive preliminary flourish
rubrics_metrics.description: But if I am to write a letter, let me begin, and not stand flourishing like a fencer at a fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing an epistle, start the substantive letter promptly rather than indulging in performative preliminaries or ornamental hesitation that delay the communicative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the story's natural power; subordinate overt purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural power of a story is diminished when the uppermost purpose in the writer seems to be to recommend something else,—namely, Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing didactic aims or explicit exhortation (e.g., frequent direct quotations to prove a point) to dominate a narrative; moral or religious content should often be 'silent' within the work rather than obtrusively quoted or preached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix fictional colouring with factual records in advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: I think it was injudicious to mix stories, avowedly colored by fiction, with the sad, true statements from the parliamentary records, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works intended to document social wrongs or marshal factual evidence (e.g., parliamentary records), keep fictionalized elements separate, because blending the two undermines credibility and the force of the factual material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine success depends on editorial hands, not gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: If they set up against the 'New Monthly', they must change their present hands. It is not tying the dead carcase of a review to a half-dead magazine will do their business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raising price or increasing the number of contributors is insufficient; periodicals need capable, energetic editors and a change of editorial tone/management rather than cosmetic fixes to compete successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose titles/mottos appropriate to tone and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You must not take my ironical one, because your book, I take it, is too serious for it... Your own 'Vigils' is perhaps the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a title or motto that matches the seriousness and sensibility of the work and its intended readers; ironic or mismatched titles harm reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sincerity over calculated advantage in dedications
rubrics_metrics.description: Some friend told him, 'This dedication will do you no good,'—i.e., not in the world's repute... 'That is a reason for doing it,' quoth Irving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dedication or public acknowledgment should be guided by honest feeling and gratitude rather than solely by considerations of worldly advantage; doing something because it won't benefit you can be a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force composition; wait for a genial impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot write without a genial impulse, and I have none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb asserts that effective literary composition depends on a genuine, genial impulse; attempting to 'spur' production when that impulse is absent often yields poor work, so patience or waiting for temperament to return is appropriate.
